204.title: Not to be served (Mark 10:32–45)
204.hook: James and John want the best seats; he came to serve and give his life
204.carry: not to be served, but to serve
204.howItsDone: Christians often call Mark 10:45 a summary of Jesus's mission, and some churches describe their ministries of service with its words; some leaders wash feet or serve meals to others as a sign of it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a camel and a needle, and the line all things are possible. What did you manage to give away? Day two hundred four.

They're on the road going up to Jerusalem now, and Jesus is walking out in front. Mark says the disciples were amazed, and the ones following were afraid. He takes the twelve aside and tells them, for the third time, and this time step by step: he'll be condemned, handed over to the Gentiles, mocked, scourged, spat on and killed, and the third day rise again. And right then, James and John come up to him with a request. Their opening line is a kid asking a parent to agree before hearing the question. "Master, we would that thou shouldest do for us whatsoever we shall desire." What is it? Let us sit, one on your right and one on your left, in your glory. The best seats. Reserved.
screen: `ON THE ROAD UP TO JERUSALEM.` → `A THIRD WARNING.` → `SAVE US THE BEST SEATS.`

segments.voice: Jesus answers them: you don't know what you're asking. Can you drink the cup I drink? We can, they say, quickly. And he says: you will. But the seats aren't mine to give. When the other ten hear about it, Mark says they were much displeased with James and John. So Jesus calls them all together. You know how rulers among the nations lord it over people, and the powerful throw their weight around. But it shall not be so among you. Whoever wants to be great must be your servant, and whoever wants to be first must be the slave of all. And then the sentence that sums it up: "For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many." Ministered unto means served. He came not to be served, but to serve. And today's word, ransom. In Greek, lytron: the price paid to set someone free, a captive or a slave. Christians have understood this word in different ways. Christian tradition hears it at the heart of the cross: Jesus's death sets people free from sin. Theologians have long asked who, if anyone, is paid; some say the picture is about the cost of freedom, not a bill handed to someone. The verse itself keeps the direction: the one who could claim the top seat gives his life for many. A few chapters on, Mark will show who ends up on his right and his left. It won't be what James and John had in mind.
screen: `CAN YE DRINK OF THE CUP?` · `IT SHALL NOT BE SO AMONG YOU.` · `NOT TO BE SERVED, BUT TO SERVE.` · `RANSOM: THE PRICE OF FREEDOM.` · then, large: `TO GIVE HIS LIFE A RANSOM FOR MANY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan to take the lowest seat. Settle, and breathe. Picture a place you'll be today. A table, a meeting, a car, a line. Where's the best seat, the first turn, the last word? Now picture yourself choosing the other one, on purpose, without making a show of it. The back of the line. The middle seat. Serving the food before sitting down. Notice what that's like. If you pray, you can offer it as a small way of following. The bell holds the time.
Ransom. In Greek, lytron: the price paid to set a captive free. He came to give his life as a ransom for many.
Your line: not to be served, but to serve. Today, take the lowest seat once, on purpose. Day two hundred four.

what a scholar hears: lytron, from lyō, to loose. and who, if anyone, is paid is an old question among theologians.

205.title: Bartimaeus (Mark 10:46–52)
205.hook: a blind beggar shouts louder when told to hush, and Jesus asks: what do you want?
205.howItsDone: Bartimaeus's cry, "Jesus, thou son of David, have mercy on me," is close to the Jesus Prayer that Orthodox and many other Christians repeat, and many Christians bring their plain requests to God in prayer as he did.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was ransom, the price that sets a captive free. Your line was not to be served, but to serve. Did you take the lowest seat? Day two hundred five.
screen: `NOT TO BE SERVED, BUT TO SERVE.`

segments.voice: Jericho, the last town before the long climb up to Jerusalem. Pilgrims are streaming through for the Passover, and Jesus is leaving town with a big crowd. By the side of the road sits a blind beggar. Mark even gives us his name: Bartimaeus, son of Timaeus. He hears it's Jesus of Nazareth passing, and he starts shouting. In the King James Bible: "Jesus, thou son of David, have mercy on me." And people around him do what people do. Shh. Not now. Don't embarrass us. You know that feeling, being told your need is too loud, too much, badly timed. And Mark says he cried the more a great deal. He shouts louder. Son of David, have mercy on me.
screen: `JERICHO, THE LAST TOWN.` → `SON OF DAVID, HAVE MERCY.` → `TOLD TO HUSH, HE SHOUTS LOUDER.`

segments.voice: And Jesus stops. The whole crowd, going up to Jerusalem, stops because one blind man wouldn't be quiet. Jesus says: call him. And the same people who were shushing him turn around: "Be of good comfort, rise; he calleth thee." Bartimaeus throws off his cloak, jumps up and comes. For a beggar, that cloak may have been his blanket and the cloth he caught coins on. He leaves it on the road. Then Jesus asks him a question that sounds almost too obvious: "What wilt thou that I should do unto thee?" Listen closely, because we've heard it before. Just a few verses ago he asked James and John the very same thing: what do you want me to do for you? They asked for the best seats in glory. This man asks for one thing, plainly: "Lord, that I might receive my sight." In Mark's Greek, the word he uses isn't Lord. It's Rabbouni, my teacher, a warm, personal word. Jesus says: go your way, your faith has made you whole. And immediately he sees, and he follows Jesus on the road. Notice three things. He's the only person Mark ever names in a healing. He's the first in Mark to call Jesus son of David, the title of Israel's king, just as they reach Jerusalem. And he's blind, yet he sees who Jesus is more clearly than the friends who asked for thrones. Two blind men frame this whole stretch of the road: one who saw men like trees, slowly, and this one, who sees at once and follows.
screen: `JESUS STOPS: CALL HIM.` · `HE THROWS OFF HIS CLOAK.` · `THE SAME QUESTION AS JAMES AND JOHN.` · `NAMED, AND FOLLOWING ON THE ROAD.` · then, large: `WHAT WILT THOU THAT I SHOULD DO UNTO THEE?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say exactly what you want. Settle, and breathe. Imagine someone who loves you stopping everything and asking, what do you want? Not what you think you should want. Not a list. One thing, plainly, the way Bartimaeus said it. Maybe it's healing. Maybe it's courage, or a job, or for someone to come home. Find the words. If you pray, you can say it to God, just as plainly. If you don't, say it quietly to yourself, and notice how it feels to name it. The bell holds the time.
Bartimaeus. Son of Timaeus, a blind beggar at Jericho who wouldn't be hushed, who asked for his sight, and who followed on the road.
Your line: what do you want? Today, when someone asks you that, even about lunch, answer honestly and plainly. Day two hundred five.

206.title: The borrowed colt (Mark 11:1–11)
206.hook: the Lord has need of it: the entry into Jerusalem on an unridden colt
206.carry: the lord has need of it
206.tomorrow: the fig tree and the temple
206.howItsDone: Christians remember this entry on Palm Sunday, the start of Holy Week; in churches that keep the day, people carry palm branches in procession and sing hosanna, and the palms are sometimes kept and later burned for the next year's Ash Wednesday.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bartimaeus shouted louder and was asked a plain question. Your line was what do you want? Did you answer someone honestly? Day two hundred six.

Two strangers walk up to a car in a driveway, unlock it, and start to drive off. The owner runs out: what are you doing? They say one sentence, and the owner lets them go. That's roughly what happens here. Jesus and his friends reach the Mount of Olives, just outside Jerusalem. He sends two of them into the village ahead: you'll find a colt tied up that no one has ever ridden. Untie it and bring it. And if anyone asks why, in the King James Bible, "say ye that the Lord hath need of him; and straightway he will send him hither." So they go. It's there, tied by a door in the street. People standing by ask: what are you doing, untying that colt? They give the answer. And the people let them go.
screen: `AT THE MOUNT OF OLIVES.` → `UNTIE IT AND BRING IT.` → `THE LORD HATH NEED OF HIM.`

segments.voice: Who owned the colt? Mark doesn't say. A friend, maybe, or someone who'd been told ahead; the text is silent. What it keeps is the loan: someone let go of something valuable, on a single sentence, because the Lord had need of it. Then the procession. They throw their garments on the colt, and Jesus sits on it. People spread their garments on the road, and others, in the King James words, cut down branches off the trees. Notice Mark doesn't say palms. That detail comes from John's Gospel, and it's where Palm Sunday gets its name. And the crowd shouts: "Hosanna; Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord." Hosanna comes from Hebrew, and it means something like save, please. In the crowd's mouth here, it rings out like praise. The words echo Psalm 118. Why a colt, and not a warhorse? Matthew and John quote the prophet Zechariah: your king comes to you, lowly, riding on a donkey. Mark doesn't quote it, but some readers hear it anyway. A king, but not the kind who arrives on a stallion. And then Mark's ending. After all the shouting, he goes into the temple, looks around at everything, and since it's late, walks back out to Bethany with the twelve. No speech. Just a long look. Christians remember this day as Palm Sunday, the start of Holy Week, and in churches that keep it, people carry palms or branches and sing hosanna.
screen: `WHO OWNED IT? MARK IS SILENT.` · `GARMENTS AND BRANCHES ON THE ROAD.` · `HOSANNA: SAVE, PLEASE.` · `A LONG LOOK, THEN BETHANY.` · then, large: `BLESSED IS HE THAT COMETH IN THE NAME OF THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find something to lend freely. Settle, and breathe. Picture the things you keep tied up by your own front door. Your car. Your tools. Your good pan. Your time on Saturday. Your spare room. Who could use one of them? Picture untying it and letting it go, no fuss, no conditions, trusting it to come back. Notice what makes you hesitate, and be gentle with that. If you pray, you can offer what you have to God's use. The bell holds the time.
The borrowed colt. Lent on one sentence, never ridden before, carrying Jesus into Jerusalem.
Your line: the lord has need of it. Today, lend something freely to someone who needs it, and don't make them ask twice. Day two hundred six.

screen: `DAY 206 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE FIG TREE AND THE TEMPLE.`

207.title: The fig tree and the temple (Mark 11:12–19)
207.word: The fig tree and the temple
207.hook: Mark sandwiches a barren fig tree around the temple scene: a house of prayer for all nations
207.carry: a house of prayer for all
207.howItsDone: Some churches pray for the nations of the world in their weekly prayers, and the temple scene is often read during Holy Week, remembering Jesus's words that God's house is for all people.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a borrowed colt, and your line was the lord has need of it. What did you lend? Day two hundred seven.

The next morning, walking in from Bethany, Jesus is hungry. Far off he sees a fig tree in full leaf, and goes to see if there's anything on it. Nothing. Only leaves. And then Mark adds a short line that readers keep tripping over: "for the time of figs was not yet." It wasn't even the season. And Jesus speaks to the tree: no one will ever eat fruit from you again. And, Mark says, his disciples heard it. Fruit out of season? It's a fair question to ask of the story. Hold on to that puzzle. Mark is a storyteller who likes to make sandwiches: he starts one story, cuts into the middle of it with another, and then finishes the first. The fig tree is the bread. Here comes the filling.
screen: `HUNGRY, AND A FIG TREE.` → `ONLY LEAVES. NOT THE SEASON.` → `A MARK SANDWICH.`

segments.voice: They come into Jerusalem, and Jesus goes into the temple courts and starts throwing people out, the buyers and the sellers. He overturns the tables of the money changers and the seats of the people selling doves. In the Law of Moses, doves were the offering for someone who couldn't afford a lamb. And Mark adds that he wouldn't let anyone carry goods through the temple, as if it were a shortcut. Then he teaches, with two old prophets in his mouth. In the King James Bible: "Is it not written, My house shall be called of all nations the house of prayer? but ye have made it a den of thieves." The first half is Isaiah: a house of prayer for all nations, foreigners included. Matthew and Luke, telling the same scene, leave out those words, of all nations. Mark keeps them. Some readers think the trading filled the outer court, where people who weren't Jewish could come to pray. The second half is Jeremiah. A den of thieves isn't where robbers rob. It's the hideout they run back to, to feel safe. Jesus is standing where Israel's prophets stood, speaking from inside his own tradition about his own temple. The chief priests and scribes hear, and start looking for a way to destroy him, because the crowds are spellbound. And now back to the bread: the fig tree. Some readers see it as a sign acted out, a picture of the temple scene. Plenty of leaves, lots of activity, and no fruit. Mark doesn't explain; he sets them side by side and lets us look.
screen: `TABLES AND DOVES OVERTURNED.` · `ISAIAH: FOR ALL NATIONS.` · `JEREMIAH: A ROBBERS' HIDEOUT.` · `LEAVES, BUT NO FRUIT.` · then, large: `MY HOUSE SHALL BE CALLED OF ALL NATIONS THE HOUSE OF PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: widen the circle. Settle, and breathe. Picture a map of the world, and let your attention travel slowly across it. Your own town. Your country. A place in the news this week. A place you've never thought about at all. Imagine all of them welcome in one house of prayer. If you pray, you can pray for the nations, one place at a time, by name. If you don't, simply wish each place well as you pass over it. The bell holds the time.
The fig tree and the temple. Mark's sandwich: a tree with leaves and no fruit, wrapped around a house meant for all nations.
screen: `THE FIG TREE AND THE TEMPLE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: a house of prayer for all. Today, notice who's missing from the places you gather, and make room for one of them. Day two hundred seven.

208.title: Faith that moves mountains (Mark 11:20–25)
208.hook: have faith in God, and when you pray, forgive
208.howItsDone: Some Christians make a habit of forgiving others before they pray, and in some churches people exchange a sign of peace before communion, echoing Jesus's words that forgiveness comes before prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fig tree and the temple, and your line was a house of prayer for all. Who did you make room for? Day two hundred eight.

A dead tree by the roadside, the morning after. Walking in from Bethany again, they pass yesterday's fig tree, and it's dried up from the roots. Peter remembers, and points, a little stunned. In the King James Bible: "Master, behold, the fig tree which thou cursedst is withered away." You can hear him wanting an explanation. What was that about? What does it mean? What was the lesson? And Jesus doesn't talk about fig trees at all. He doesn't explain the temple either. He starts talking about prayer, and about a mountain. And then, when you'd expect him to finish with something grand, he ends somewhere very small and very close to home. Somewhere as close as the people you live with.
screen: `THE SAME ROAD, NEXT MORNING.` → `WITHERED FROM THE ROOTS.` → `WHAT DOES IT MEAN?`

segments.voice: Jesus begins with four words: "Have faith in God." Then the big picture: whoever says to this mountain, be lifted up and thrown into the sea, and doesn't doubt in their heart, it will happen. They're walking near the Mount of Olives, within sight of the temple mount. Moving a mountain was a way of saying doing the impossible; later Jewish teachers praised a brilliant rabbi as an uprooter of mountains. Then he goes further: whatever you ask for in prayer, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours. This is a verse people have leaned on and argued over. Some Christians hear a bold promise to pray big. Others warn against treating it like a vending machine, and read it next to other places where Jesus prays that God's will be done. Some hold the two together: pray boldly, and trust. But look at the very next sentence: "And when ye stand praying, forgive, if ye have ought against any: that your Father also which is in heaven may forgive you your trespasses." Right after the mountain, the condition isn't more faith. It's forgiveness. In Mark, the letting go comes before the asking. The Greek word for forgive here, aphiēmi, also means to release, to let go, like opening your hand and dropping something. Mark uses the same verb back in chapter one, when the fishermen leave their nets. The fig tree without fruit, the temple without prayer, and now this: some readers hear one lesson in all three, that the fruit Jesus looks for starts close to home, with a grudge put down.
screen: `HAVE FAITH IN GOD.` · `A MOUNTAIN INTO THE SEA.` · `PRAY BOLDLY, AND TRUST.` · `WHEN YE STAND PRAYING, FORGIVE.` · then, large: `WHEN YE STAND PRAYING, FORGIVE, IF YE HAVE OUGHT AGAINST ANY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: forgive first. Settle, and breathe. Is there someone you have ought against, as the old English says? Someone you're holding something against, big or small? Let their face come to mind. You don't have to feel warm. You don't have to pretend it didn't matter, or call them. Just picture opening your hand, and letting the grudge drop, even for these two minutes. If you pray, you can do that first, and then bring your prayer. If you don't, just notice what your hand feels like, open. The bell holds the time.
Faith that moves mountains. Pray boldly, trust God, and before you ask, forgive.
Your line: forgive, then pray. Today, whenever you ask for something, from God or from anyone, check your hand first for a grudge. Day two hundred eight.

209.title: By what authority? (Mark 11:27–33)
209.hook: leaders try to trap him, and he answers with a question
209.howItsDone: Christians often notice how many questions Jesus asks in the Gospels, and some Bible study groups use his questions, like "who do you say I am?", as prompts for honest discussion.

segments.voice: Yesterday, faith that moves mountains, and a surprising condition. Your line was forgive, then pray. Did you check your hand for a grudge? Day two hundred nine.

"Have you stopped being late all the time?" Some questions aren't really questions. Whatever you say, you lose. Jesus is back in Jerusalem, walking in the temple courts, the day after he overturned the tables. And a delegation arrives: the chief priests, the scribes and the elders. In the King James Bible they ask: "By what authority doest thou these things? and who gave thee this authority to do these things?" It's a trap with two jaws. If he says God gave it to me, they could call it blasphemy. If he says no one, then he's just a troublemaker from Galilee. And the crowd is listening.
screen: `A QUESTION THAT'S A TRAP.` → `THE COUNCIL ARRIVES.` → `WHO GAVE THEE THIS AUTHORITY?`

segments.voice: Jesus says: let me ask you one question. Answer me, and I'll tell you by what authority I do these things. Then: "The baptism of John, was it from heaven, or of men? answer me." Now they're the ones in the trap. They huddle. If we say from heaven, he'll say, then why didn't you believe him? If we say from men, the crowd will turn on us, because, as Mark puts it, all men counted John a prophet indeed. So they give the safest answer there is: "We cannot tell." We don't know. And Jesus says: "Neither do I tell you by what authority I do these things." Notice this isn't a dodge. His question and theirs are the same question. John had baptized him, and the voice from heaven had spoken at that very moment. If they could be honest about John, they'd have their answer about Jesus. Jesus answers with a question again and again in the Gospels. Who do you say I am? What do you want? Why are you afraid? A good question doesn't close the conversation. It hands it back and asks you to be honest. Mark lets us overhear what the leaders weigh: the crowd, not John. The word for authority in Greek is exousia: the right, and the power, to act.
screen: `LET ME ASK YOU ONE QUESTION.` · `JOHN: FROM HEAVEN, OR OF MEN?` · `WE CANNOT TELL.` · `A QUESTION HANDS IT BACK.` · then, large: `NEITHER DO I TELL YOU BY WHAT AUTHORITY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find a good question. Settle, and breathe. Think of a hard question someone's been pressing on you. At work, at home, in your own head. Instead of rushing to answer it, ask what question lies underneath. What are you really asking? What would help? What do you think? What are you afraid of? Find one honest question you could hand back, not to escape, but to open things up. If you pray, you can bring God your own hardest question. The bell holds the time.
By what authority? The leaders' trap, answered with a question about John that they were afraid to answer honestly.
Your line: answer with a question. Today, when someone asks you something hard, ask one good question back before you answer. Day two hundred nine.

210.title: The vineyard tenants (Mark 12:1–12)
210.hook: the stone the builders rejected becomes the cornerstone
210.howItsDone: Christians often call Jesus the cornerstone, drawing on this psalm, and many churches mark the laying of a building's cornerstone with a service; many churches today also teach explicitly against reading this parable as a rejection of the Jewish people.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a trap in the temple courts, and your line was answer with a question. Did you hand one good question back? Day two hundred ten. The end of the week.

Still in the temple courts, with the leaders still listening, Jesus tells a story. A man plants a vineyard. He builds a hedge around it, digs a winepress, puts up a watchtower. Anyone who knew their scriptures would hear Isaiah, whose song pictured Israel as God's vineyard. Then the owner rents it to tenants and goes away. At harvest he sends a servant to collect his share. They beat him and send him off empty. He sends another; they hit him on the head. Another; they kill him. Many more, beaten or killed. He has one left: his son, his beloved. Surely they'll respect my son. And the tenants look at each other. This is the heir. Kill him, and it's all ours.
screen: `A VINEYARD, A HEDGE, A TOWER.` → `SERVANT AFTER SERVANT.` → `LAST OF ALL, THE BELOVED SON.`

segments.voice: They kill him and throw him out of the vineyard. What will the owner do? He'll come and put an end to those tenants and give the vineyard to others. Then Jesus quotes a psalm, in the King James Bible: "The stone which the builders rejected is become the head of the corner." Picture builders sorting stones, tossing one onto the rubbish heap as useless. Later, that very stone turns out to be the one holding the corners of the whole building together. It's from Psalm 118, the same psalm the crowds had sung days earlier: blessed is he that cometh. Many readers point out a wordplay in Hebrew, where son is ben and stone is even. The son they reject becomes the stone everything rests on. Christians hear the whole story of Jesus in it: sent last, beloved, rejected, killed, and made the cornerstone. Mark says the leaders understood he'd told it against them, and wanted to arrest him, but feared the crowd, so they left. It's important to read that carefully. This parable has sometimes been misused to claim God rejected the Jewish people. Mark himself points it at a handful of leaders, while the crowd, Jewish too, stands with Jesus. Many churches today say plainly that the anti-Jewish reading is wrong. Now look back at the week. Ransom, and not to be served but to serve. Bartimaeus asked what do you want. A borrowed colt. A fig tree and a temple. Faith that moves mountains, and forgive, then pray. A question answered with a question. And the rejected stone. All week, the road has been leading to one place, and the stone is part of what's waiting there.
